title: China's Private-Sector Botnets Are Worth Disrupting
gist: DOJ disrupted two Chinese state-linked botnets (QScan/QTRouter) run by a private Chinese contractor for MSS/PLA, the third such disruption since Dec 2023, but historical patterns show China's IoT botnet infrastructure regenerates faster than the U.S. can permanently dismantle it; separately, a Trump administration policy unleashing private-sector hackers on cybercriminals and an underfunded federal water-security pilot both signal shifting, resource-constrained U.S. cyber-defense posture.

insights.claim: The FBI disrupted QScan and QTRouter, two botnet components run by QTFY, a group operating for Chinese private company Nanjing Xinjiuwei Network Technology, whose customers include China's Ministry of State Security and the People's Liberation Army.
insights.speaker: Tom Uren
insights.so_what: Confirms China systematically outsources state cyberespionage infrastructure to nominally private firms, a model likely to recur and complicating attribution/sanctions targeting for policymakers and cyber-insurers.
insights.quote: QTFY customers include China's Ministry of State Security and the People's Liberation Army.

insights.claim: QTFY's targets alleged in the FBI affidavit included federal government agencies, the U.S. Senate, and private-sector hospitals, telecommunications companies, and financial institutions.
insights.speaker: Tom Uren
insights.so_what: Signals critical-infrastructure and financial-sector operators should expect continued targeting from Chinese state-linked botnets and should treat IoT device hygiene as a material risk factor.
insights.locator: paragraph on QTFY customers and targets

insights.claim: This is the third Chinese state-backed botnet the U.S. government has disrupted since December 2023, following the KV botnet (active from Feb 2022, disrupted Dec 2023, linked to Volt Typhoon) and Raptor Train (formed May 2020, disrupted Sept 2024 after four and a half years, linked to Flax Typhoon).
insights.speaker: Tom Uren
insights.so_what: Establishes a base rate: Chinese state-linked botnets historically run undetected for 2-4.5 years, implying a large population of currently-undetected active networks investors and CISOs should assume exist right now.
insights.quote: Two years of active use before detection seems like a pretty good run.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'The first to be disrupted was the KV botnet'

insights.claim: QTFY backhauls its traffic into China using paid 'high-tier corporate subscriptions' to Chinese commercial VPN service Fastlink rather than compromising additional relay devices, because it's operationally easier.
insights.speaker: Tom Uren
insights.so_what: Commercial VPN providers used as state-cyberespionage backhaul are a plausible future sanctions/disruption target and a due-diligence flag for any firm doing business with Chinese VPN vendors.
insights.locator: paragraph on backhauling traffic via Fastlink

insights.claim: Since the KV botnet was disrupted in late 2023, a related JDY botnet has more than doubled in size, according to Lumen.
insights.speaker: Tom Uren
insights.so_what: Direct evidence that takedowns produce only temporary disruption; sister networks absorb capacity, meaning defenders should budget for a persistent, expanding threat rather than a one-time fix.
insights.quote: a sister network known as the JDY botnet has more than doubled in size

insights.claim: The author frames the ongoing dynamic as a 'discover, disrupt, rebuild, and hack cycle' in which the U.S. wins individual battles but China has not lost the broader war.
insights.speaker: Tom Uren
insights.so_what: Useful framework for investors assessing cyber-risk exposure: treat botnet takedowns as tactical wins, not risk-eliminating events, when pricing cyber-insurance or infrastructure resilience.
insights.quote: The U.S. won this week's battle, but China hasn't lost the war.

themes.theme: U.S. shift to offensive private-sector cyber response

insights.claim: The Qilin ransomware-as-a-service group, per the International Cyber Digest, briefly published 6.3 GB of data it claims was stolen from the U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), including investigation-target names, phone numbers, IP addresses, and mobile forensic data.
insights.speaker: Tom Uren
insights.so_what: A confirmed breach of a federal law-enforcement CALEA/lawful-access system by a Russian-speaking ransomware crew raises the stakes for U.S. retaliatory cyber policy and is a live test case for the administration's new private-hacker initiative.

insights.claim: Last month the Trump administration announced it would recruit private-sector hackers to target cybercriminals, a policy shift that makes it newly plausible the FBI or Cyber Command could prioritize retaliating against a group like Qilin, which before this policy would have been inconceivable given competing priorities.
insights.speaker: Tom Uren
insights.so_what: A material change in U.S. offensive-cyber posture; watch for follow-through actions against Qilin as an early signal of how aggressively this authority will actually be used.
insights.quote: Before this announcement, it was inconceivable that the FBI or Cyber Command would target Qilin in response.
insights.locator: ATF Hack section, paragraph on private-sector hackers

insights.claim: National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross launched Project Watershed 250, a six-month Texas pilot with a dozen companies (including Microsoft, Google, AWS, and Dragos) providing red-teaming and AI security tools to water utilities, but the program provides no additional funding.
insights.speaker: Tom Uren
insights.so_what: A free-tools-without-funding model is unlikely to move the needle for a sector that lacks staff to implement fixes — a governance/execution-risk pattern relevant to any critical-infrastructure-security investment thesis.

insights.claim: The U.S. water sector comprises roughly 50,000 community water systems, most serving fewer than 10,000 people, and most lack the resources or skills to act on security recommendations even when handed free tools.
insights.speaker: Tom Uren
insights.so_what: Structural fragmentation (50,000 tiny operators) means critical-infrastructure cyber risk in water is systemic and unlikely to be fixed by pilot programs alone — a durable tail risk for insurers and infrastructure investors.
insights.quote: 50,000 community water systems, most of which serve less than 10,000 people

insights.claim: In response to recent Iranian cyberattacks on water utilities, CISA's guidance was only basic remediation: remove targeted devices from the internet, use VPNs, enforce strong passwords, and allowlist IP addresses for remote access.
insights.speaker: Tom Uren
insights.so_what: Shows the baseline security maturity of U.S. water infrastructure is extremely low, implying continued vulnerability to state-linked (Iranian) attacks regardless of new pilot initiatives.

insights.claim: Meta's August 2026 adversarial threat report describes disrupting networks behind terrorism, fraud, and surveillance-for-hire operations, but the author suggests Meta faces conflicting incentives and could do more.
insights.speaker: Tom Uren
insights.so_what: A platform-governance signal worth tracking for social-media regulatory and reputational-risk assessments.
insights.locator: Three Reasons to Be Cheerful section

insights.claim: The Office of Management and Budget issued a memo directing public-facing federal agencies to migrate to the login.gov single sign-on platform to centralize authentication.
insights.speaker: Tom Uren
insights.so_what: A federal IT-modernization data point relevant to gov-tech and identity-security vendors tracking government authentication contracts.
insights.locator: Three Reasons to Be Cheerful section

insights.claim: An unidentified actor executed a roughly 33-hour BGP hijack of Softaculous's IP space to deliver malicious updates to users of the Virtualizor web-hosting management platform, obtaining a fraudulent TLS certificate to host a clone site.
insights.speaker: Tom Uren
insights.so_what: Illustrates BGP hijacking remains a viable supply-chain attack vector against hosting-infrastructure vendors, relevant to due diligence on web-hosting and DevOps tooling companies.
insights.locator: Risky Bulletin: BGP hijack targets Virtualizor

insights.claim: The Dutch government proposed a bill significantly expanding surveillance and offensive-hacking powers for its AIVD and MIVD intelligence services, citing the threat of war with Russia and rising aggressiveness from China and Iran.
insights.speaker: Tom Uren
insights.so_what: Part of a broader European trend toward expanded state surveillance/offensive-cyber authority in response to great-power threats, relevant to EU tech-regulation and defense-policy tracking.
